clue.text: Constable initially spots collision

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word Constable

parts.note: a rash is an outbreak of spots on the skin

explanation.surface: A policeman notices a road accident.
explanation.definitionFit: A crash is a violent collision, as between vehicles.

clue.text: Charge nothing and shock troops

parts.note: to command is to order, and charge can mean to instruct
O looks like zero, meaning nothing

explanation.surface: Elite soldiers attack without charging anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Commandos are soldiers trained for raids, the kind of troops used for shock attacks.

clue.text: What a sticker the man is in a low bar!

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the man sits inside the low bar

parts.note: a dive is a disreputable bar
he's is the contraction of he is, the man being he

explanation.surface: Exclaiming over a regular who won't leave a seedy bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sticker' is a person who stays put in the surface, but in the answer it is a label: adhesive is what a sticker uses.
explanation.definitionFit: Adhesive is glue, which is what a sticker has on its back to make it stick.

clue.text: From poisonous plant, woman's giving first of berries to Marlowe

parts.note: her is the possessive for a woman

indicators.note: first of picks the opening letter of the word berries

parts.note: Christopher Marlowe was the Elizabethan playwright

explanation.surface: A woman feeds toxic berries to the playwright Marlowe.
explanation.definitionFit: Herb Christopher is baneberry, a woodland plant whose berries are poisonous.

clue.text: A new chief is beginning to track revolutionary

parts.note: arch as a prefix or adjective means chief, as in arch-enemy
taken as written

indicators.note: beginning to signals the first letter of the following word, track

explanation.surface: A newly appointed leader starts out on the road to revolt.
explanation.definitionFit: An anarchist seeks to overthrow all government, so is a revolutionary by nature.

clue.text: Church's part in error left out

indicators.note: out means the letter for left is removed

parts.note: a lapse is a slip or error

explanation.surface: Part of a church was left out by mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is the rounded section at the east end of a church, so a part of a church.

clue.text: A timeless invention supported by business freak

indicators.note: in a down clue, supported by means placed above, so business comes below
timeless means without T, the abbreviation for time

parts.note: fiction is something invented or made up
ado means fuss or business, as in much ado

explanation.surface: An eternal invention is backed by a fanatical businessman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'timeless' removes T, the abbreviation for time, from the invention word; 'supported by' in a down clue puts business underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: A freak in the informal sense is an enthusiast, as is an aficionado.

clue.text: Descriptive of stone-waller, but not his flannels?

definitions.text: Descriptive of stone-waller, but not his flannels?

parts.words: Descriptive of stone-waller, but not his flannels?
parts.note: a stone-walling batsman defends doggedly at his crease, though his white cricket trousers get creased all the same

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a stone-waller is a batsman who blocks every ball; the crease is the line where he stands, and flannels are white cricket trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes fabric that does not wrinkle and, punningly, a batsman who holds out at his crease.

clue.text: Establish one's not out yet, we hear

indicators.note: we hear signals a word that sounds like the phrase

parts.note: a batsman who is not out yet is in still

explanation.surface: A batsman confirms he is still not out.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman who has not been dismissed is 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: To instil an idea is to establish it gradually in someone's mind.

clue.text: Improves a little steak wife cooked

indicators.note: cooked suggests the letters are messed about and rearranged

explanation.surface: A wife cooks a steak to make it slightly better.
explanation.definitionFit: Tweaks are small adjustments, so something that tweaks improves it a little.

clue.text: Indian sage gives Irish ham a difference

indicators.note: giving the letters a difference means making them different, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A guru supposedly alters the taste of some Irish ham.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gives ... a difference' is the anagram signal: the nine letters of IRISH HAM A are reshuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: A maharishi is a Hindu teacher or holy man, a title for a revered Indian sage.

clue.text: Come after guarantee has run out

indicators.note: out means the letter for run is dropped from the word for guarantee

parts.note: to ensure something is to guarantee it
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Something follows once a warranty has expired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has run out' reads as an expired guarantee; in fact 'run' gives R and 'out' removes it from ENSURE.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensue is to follow on afterwards, so it means to come after something.

clue.text: A fabric without the first trace of style in area of France

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the fabric wraps around the letter

parts.note: lace is a delicate openwork fabric

indicators.note: the first trace of a word is its opening letter, here from style

explanation.surface: A stylish lace from some French region turns out to lack style after all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking' but means 'outside': LACE goes round S.
explanation.definitionFit: Alsace is a historic region in north-eastern France, bordering Germany.

clue.text: Impudence by staff offered to one's face

parts.note: lip is informal for cheeky talk or impudence
a staff is a walking stick

explanation.surface: Cheek and a wooden staff are offered right in front of someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' simply places the two pieces side by side; 'offered to one's face' is a playful definition of make-up applied to the lips.
explanation.definitionFit: Lipstick is cosmetic colour that is put onto the face, specifically on the lips.

clue.text: Plan to install one simple ignition system

indicators.note: to install means to put inside, so the plan takes in the letter for one

parts.note: a plot is a plan or scheme
I is the Roman numeral one
light means easy or simple, as in light reading

explanation.surface: A scheme to fit a straightforward ignition device.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilot light is a small permanent flame used to ignite a gas burner, so an ignition system.

clue.text: Translation accepted by journal is distracting

indicators.note: accepted by means taken in by, so the journal word holds the translation

parts.note: a diary is a daily journal
a version is a rendering of a text in another language

explanation.surface: A translated piece being published in a journal causes distraction.
explanation.definitionFit: Something diversionary draws attention away, which is what distracting means.

clue.text: Insect repellent — that's not new in, say, July party

indicators.note: that's not means the following letter is taken away

parts.note: July is an example of a month
a ball is a formal dancing party

explanation.surface: A summer party needs something to keep the bugs away.
explanation.definitionFit: A mothball is a ball of camphor or naphthalene put among clothes to repel moths.

clue.text: Left seaside distressed, with nothing in mind

indicators.note: distressed means damaged or upset, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone left the seaside upset and with a blank mind.
explanation.definitionFit: Idealess means lacking ideas, so having nothing in mind.

clue.text: Very well-behaved, very nearly getting medal

parts.note: as good as means practically or very nearly
gold is the winner's medal

explanation.surface: A well-behaved athlete is on the brink of winning a medal.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a child who is behaving perfectly, so very well-behaved.

clue.text: Caution about being taken in by confidence trick

indicators.note: being taken in by means placed inside, so the word for about sits within the trick

parts.note: a scam is a swindle or con
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A warning about getting caught by a con man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caution' looks like a warning, but in informal British English a caution is a very funny person, as is a scream.
explanation.definitionFit: Both caution and scream are informal terms for a hilariously amusing person.

clue.text: A minor route on the Continent

parts.note: in British road classification, the letter B marks secondary roads below the main A roads

explanation.surface: Taking a back road while travelling in Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain, A roads are main roads and B roads are smaller ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Abroad means in a foreign country, and for Britons the Continent means mainland Europe.

clue.text: Group needs transport, endless great quantity

parts.note: a cab is a taxi, a form of transport

indicators.note: endless means the final letter of the word for great quantity is cut off

parts.note: oodles means a great quantity

explanation.surface: A party needs a vehicle and plenty of other things.
explanation.definitionFit: A caboodle is a collection or lot, as in the whole kit and caboodle, so a group.

clue.text: A maths failure causing complaint

indicators.note: a failure is a breakdown, so the letters of the fodder are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Failing a maths exam brings on a medical complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: The A stays in place at the front; 'failure' scrambles only MATHS to give STHMA.
explanation.definitionFit: Asthma is a respiratory illness, and complaint can mean an ailment.

clue.text: One found mostly up trunk?

indicators.note: mostly means all but the last letter is kept
in a down clue, up means the word trunk is read from bottom to top

explanation.surface: Something is typically located on a tree trunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns TRUNK into KNURT and 'mostly' drops its final T. The whole clue also defines it: a knot found on a trunk.
explanation.definitionFit: A knur is a knot or gnarled growth on a tree trunk.

clue.text: Age record pursued by old companion

indicators.note: pursued by means followed by, so the record comes first and the rest after

parts.note: EP stands for extended play, a type of record
CH stands for Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: An age-old record is chased by a former friend.
explanation.definitionFit: An epoch is a long period of history, which is one sense of an age.

clue.text: Snare Buckingham, for one, into gaudy drinking-house

parts.note: a gin is a trap or snare for game
Buckingham Palace, the London home of the monarch, is an example of a palace

explanation.surface: Someone plans to lure people into a flashy pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' looks like a container signal but is only a link; Buckingham Palace is the monarch's London residence.
explanation.definitionFit: A gin palace was a showily decorated Victorian pub, so a gaudy drinking-house.

clue.text: Teenager once right about the time to find a minister

indicators.note: about means around, so the teenager and right go around the time and to

parts.note: a Mod was a member of a 1960s British youth movement
an era is a period of time
taken as written

explanation.surface: A former youth tries to find a vicar at the right moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts teenager-plus-right around the time-plus-to. Mods were a 1960s British youth cult; a Church of Scotland moderator is a minister.
explanation.definitionFit: The Moderator presides over the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland and is a minister.

clue.text: Stories are provided for defective juries

definitions.meaning: in law, a writ summoning people to make up a jury that lacks members

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is legal Latin: extra jurors called to fill a short panel, known as talesmen.
explanation.definitionFit: Tales are stories, and in old law the word named the extra jurors summoned to complete a jury.
